extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and research funders interested in peer review quality, bias, and policy design
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating mechanisms, measurement, and policy responses for bias and disagreement in scientific peer review (empirical study of PLOS ONE neuroscience reviews). Useful for designing reviewer selection and editorial policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity-only review
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS ONE evaluates manuscripts only on whether claims are valid; reviewers are instructed to assess completed manuscripts on scientific correctness alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This review process was designed specifically to rule out subjective review criteria and minimize competition (PLOS ONE accepts ~70% of submissions). Despite these instructions, validity-oriented review did not materially reduce disagreement or eliminate favoritism in the observed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer compliance with review instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may fail to comply with instructions to evaluate only scientific validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be able to identify non-compliant reviewers and either train them or exclude them from future invitations; non-compliance remains a possible mechanism driving bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish nepotism versus schools-of-thought mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary explanations for favoritism are nepotism (favoring close connections for self-benefit) and schools of thought (shared epistemic/methodological commitments leading to favoritism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nepotism should be most salient in competitive, zero-sum environments; schools of thought predict bias that varies smoothly with network proximity. Empirical patterns (e.g., distant reviewers more favorable than very distant) were taken as more consistent with schools of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal of closely connected reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy that recuses reviewers who are most closely connected to authors (e.g., co-authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a sensible response to the assumption that only close reviewers are corrupted by nepotism, but the study finds bias extends beyond close ties, so recusal of just the closest connections may be insufficient to eliminate favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify reviewers across co-authorship clusters (schools of thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit reviewers from different co-authorship clusters/schools of thought to achieve fairer evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers representing different schools should be able to surface differing assumptions and reveal how crucial those differences are; editors and funders who value validity and diversity should value diverse evaluators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise versus bias trade-off in reviewer selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting reviewers is conceptualized as a trade-off between expertise (better discrimination) and bias (favoring own area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For evaluations of completed work with high-expertise reviewers, the practical choice may be between a 'positive' expert inside the author's school of thought and a 'negative' expert outside it — not simply between expert-biased and unbiased but less expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability / disagreement as evaluation metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of agreement among reviewers (inter-rater reliability). The study reports inter-rater reliability = 0.19 for PLOS ONE reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in a validity-only review setting, reviewers disagreed as often as in conventional settings that use subjective criteria; inter-rater reliability is therefore a key metric for assessing how subjective a review system is in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-authorship distance as predictor of reviewer favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure reviewer-author proximity in the co-authorship network and relate it to review outcomes: each increased step of co-authorship proximity gives authors a bonus of 0.11 points on a 4-point scale; close reviewers rarely reject (7.1%) while most distant reject >20% (20.4%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize distance as levels (close = co-authors, distant = co-authors of co-authors, very distant = 3+). Use regression models (e.g., OLS with manuscript fixed effects and reviewer controls) to estimate the effect; interpret differences across distance steps to evaluate mechanisms (nepotism vs schools of thought).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding (masking author identity) as anti-bias intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: An intervention intended to reduce nepotism by anonymizing authors to reviewers (double-blind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental evidence on blinding is inconsistent — possible reasons include reviewers guessing authors' identities or nepotism not being the dominant mechanism; blinding cannot be assumed to reliably eliminate bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of cumulative advantage in reviewer selection
rubrics_metrics.description: High-status authors tend to have more connections and larger schools of thought, which affects reviewer sampling and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting reviewers based on expertise alone may disproportionately sample from large schools, unintentionally soliciting more favorable reviews for high-status authors and producing cumulative advantage; policy design should account for this dynamic to avoid downstream status spirals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors should balance expertise and epistemic diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing reviewers, editors should weigh both reviewer expertise and the need for epistemic diversity (representation of different schools of thought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal is validity and diverse outputs, prefer a panel that balances experts from inside and outside an author's school so that substantive disagreements are made explicit to the editor or funder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological standard: control variables and fixed effects in bias estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate reviewer bias using regression models that control for reviewer characteristics (e.g., h-index, number of co-authorships) and manuscript fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper uses OLS with manuscript FE and reviewer controls; *, **, *** indicate p < .1, .05, .01. Note that models explained only a small proportion of within-manuscript score variation, reflecting constrained variation and other unexplained factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling missing co-authorship network data
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-authorship networks constructed from Scopus API are limited (returns up to 179 co-authors); missing nodes/edges bias measured distances upward, especially for distances 4+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because distances 4+ may be biased upward, recode such distances appropriately (the study recoded distances 4+); report and consider the potential measurement error when interpreting distance-based analyses.
